title: The Voice of the LORD in the Storm
summary: The psalm calls the heavenly beings to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD. It then describes a thunderstorm sweeping in from the Mediterranean, in which the voice of the LORD thunders over the waters, breaks the cedars of Lebanon, shakes the wilderness, and strips the forests, while in his temple all cry glory. The LORD sits enthroned over the flood as King forever, and he gives his people strength and peace.
story: Psalm 29 follows the laments of Psalms 26 to 28, whose speaker begged God not to be silent (28:1). Here God's voice is anything but silent; it roars through the whole created world. The psalm returns to the theme of Psalm 19, where the heavens declared God's glory without words, but here the declaration is loud and overwhelming. Its closing picture of the LORD enthroned over the flood recalls the waters of Genesis 1 and the flood of Genesis 6 to 9, and its final blessing brings that cosmic power down to the ordinary life of God's people: strength and peace.
historical:
The heading reads A Psalm of David. Traditional readers accept Davidic authorship; many modern scholars treat the heading as a collection note and see the psalm as one of the oldest in the Psalter, on the basis of its archaic poetic style. Since the discovery in 1929 of the Canaanite texts from Ugarit (modern Ras Shamra, on the Syrian coast), scholars have noticed how closely this psalm's language resembles poems about the storm god Baal: his voice is thunder, he rules the waters, he is enthroned as king, and the gods acclaim him. Some scholars have argued that Psalm 29 was adapted from a Canaanite hymn, with the LORD's name substituted for Baal's. Others think it was written in Israel as a deliberate polemic, using the neighbors' own imagery to claim that everything attributed to Baal belongs to the LORD alone. A third view holds simply that Israel and its neighbors shared a common poetic vocabulary.

The geography is specific. The storm moves from the waters (the Mediterranean) across Lebanon and Sirion (the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon, according to Deuteronomy 3:9) and on to the wilderness of Kadesh. Kadesh may be Kadesh-barnea in the far south, which would sweep the storm across the whole land, or Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria, which would keep it in the north near Lebanon.
cultural:
Storms in the eastern Mediterranean come in from the sea in autumn and winter, and they can be violent: thunder, lightning, and high winds that tear down trees. For farmers in Canaan the rains that followed were life itself, and the gods who were believed to control them were worshiped with great devotion. That is why Baal worship was such a persistent temptation for Israel (1 Kings 18). The cedars of Lebanon were famous across the ancient world for their size and strength, prized for temples and palaces, and they stood for everything grand and permanent. To picture them snapped like twigs was to show power beyond any human or natural force.

The heavenly beings of verse 1 (literally sons of gods, or sons of God) are members of God's heavenly court, the angelic beings who surround his throne (compare Job 1:6 and Psalm 89:6-7). Where the Canaanite poems have the gods acclaim Baal, this psalm summons the heavenly beings to acknowledge that glory and strength belong to the LORD.
literary: The psalm is a hymn in three movements. Verses 1 and 2 are a call to praise in the heavenly court, built on the threefold repetition of ascribe to the LORD. Verses 3 to 9 describe the storm, driven by the phrase the voice of the LORD, which appears seven times like seven peals of thunder. The storm moves geographically from the waters to Lebanon, to the wilderness, to the forests, and its effect grows from sound to shattering to shaking. Verses 10 and 11 close the psalm with the LORD's enthronement and his blessing on his people. The divine name, the LORD, appears eighteen times in eleven verses, saturating the poem. The psalm is framed by two scenes of worship: the heavenly beings ascribing glory at the start and all in his temple crying glory at the end of the storm.

outline.t: The heavenly beings called to ascribe glory to the LORD
The voice of the LORD over the waters
The voice that breaks the cedars and strikes with fire
The voice that shakes the wilderness: in his temple all cry glory
The LORD enthroned over the flood gives strength and peace

doctrines.note: The LORD rules the most powerful forces of the natural world, the sea, the storm, and the flood. He sits enthroned over them as King forever. Nothing in creation is beyond his command.

The psalm takes the imagery Canaan used for Baal and ascribes every bit of it to the LORD, denying that any other god controls the storm or the rains. It is a confession that glory belongs to one God only.
God's voice is shown as active in creation, not only at the beginning but in every storm. The world is not self-running; it responds to the word of its maker.

words.note: Qol, voice, sound, or thunder. The same word can mean a person's voice or the sound of thunder (Exodus 9:23), and the psalm plays on both. Its sevenfold repetition makes thunder the voice of God. At Sinai the people heard God's voice amid thunder (Exodus 19:16-19).

Yahav, to give or ascribe. The imperative, ascribe, opens the psalm three times. It asks not that anyone give God something he lacks, but that they acknowledge what is already his: glory and strength, and the glory due his name.

Mabbul, flood. Outside this psalm, the word is used in the Old Testament only for the great flood of Noah's time (Genesis 6 to 11). The LORD sat enthroned over that flood, the psalm says, and he remains King forever; the most terrifying waters in Israel's memory were under his rule.

Shalom, peace, wholeness, well-being. It means more than the absence of conflict; it is flourishing, everything as it should be. After all the thunder, the psalm ends with this word, the gentle gift of the God whose voice breaks cedars.

christ: The New Testament doesn't quote Psalm 29, but its picture of the LORD who rules the waters stands behind the Gospel scene in which Jesus calms the storm. He rebuked the winds and the sea, and it was perfectly calm, and the disciples asked, “What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!” (Matthew 8:26-27). For readers who knew psalms like this one, only the LORD who sits enthroned over the flood commands the storm, so the disciples' question points to who Jesus is. At Jesus' baptism a voice came from heaven (Matthew 3:17), and in John 12:28-29 the Father's voice sounded so that some in the crowd said it had thundered. The psalm ends with the LORD giving his people peace; Jesus says to his disciples that he leaves them his own peace (John 14:27). These links are thematic, but they show the New Testament assigning to Jesus the powers the psalm reserves for the LORD.

hard.q: If Psalm 29 closely resembles Canaanite poems about Baal, does that make it borrowed pagan religion?
hard.a: The resemblances are real and widely recognized: storm imagery, divine enthronement over waters, and acclamation by heavenly beings all appear in the Ugaritic texts. Scholars differ on how to explain them. Some think Israel adapted an existing hymn; others that Israel wrote its own psalm in the shared poetic language of the region; others that the psalm was a pointed polemic, taking Baal's titles and giving them to the LORD. On any of these views, the psalm does not simply repeat Canaanite religion. It names one God only, whose voice rules the storm, who is enthroned over the flood, and who gives his people strength and peace. Using the language of one's culture to confess a very different God is something biblical writers do often, as Paul later did at Athens (Acts 17:22-31). The shared imagery shows the world the psalm spoke into; the psalm's content shows how Israel's faith differed from it.

questions: The psalm hears God's voice in a thunderstorm. Where do you most sense the power and majesty of God in the world around you?
After all the thunder, the psalm ends with God giving strength and peace. How can the same God be both overwhelming and gentle?
The psalm takes what Canaan said about Baal and gives it all to the LORD. What powers in our own culture are credited with what belongs to God?
